content:
Representatives for R&B singer Christian Berishaj, known professionally as JMSN, have sent a cease-and-desist notice to Donald Trump's White House over its unauthorized use of his song "Love Me" in a controversial, taxpayer-funded ad promoting the president's 2026 midterm campaign.

In a letter sent Monday to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, JMSN's legal representatives said the song, first released in 2023, was used "without the copyright holder granting any synchronization license, master use license, or any other permission whatsoever."

The letter also added: "Even if asked, permission would not have been granted."

JMSN himself has publicly spoken out, writing on social media this week:

"For any new friends, there are two ways this can go," he wrote. "One, he or his team reaches out to me to license the song, I say 'no', and you never know about it." "Or two, the president uses the song illegally without inquiring and the public is still dumb enough to assume there's been a clearance."

"The result is clearly the latter," he added. "I have built my career independently with no support from any mainstream system and have held true to never selling out my artistic integrity. I have no management, so to be put in this position and forced to publicly respond is absurd."

The lawyer's letter was co-signed by Norm Eisen of Democracy Defenders Action, who served as ethics counsel in the Obama White House, along with representatives from the law firm Ballard Spahr LLP, demanding that the "government immediately cease and refrain from any further use of 'Love Me'" and from using any of JMSN's music going forward.

The letter notes that the White House "never sought or obtained permission" and that the move could create "a false endorsement or connection, leading the public to believe that JMSN is somehow affiliated with or associated with this administration."

The lawyers are demanding that the Trump administration "immediately withdraw it from all upcoming media schedules and notify in writing all networks, broadcast stations, cable or satellite providers, streaming platforms, and media buyers that have aired the ad to cease its broadcast."

They are also demanding that the administration "delete and take down all online versions of the ad, as well as any other videos or posts containing the song, including but not limited to those on Facebook, X, TikTok, or YouTube," and "provide written records of each broadcast and publication of the ad, including the date, time, network or station, market of broadcast, program name, and total media spend."

The lawyers demanded written confirmation by 5 p.m. ET on Thursday, Oct. 1, that the government had stopped all infringing activity.
